dated.title: UTF-8 designed on a New Jersey diner placemat
dated.detail: Ken Thompson sketched the bit-packing over dinner with Rob Pike. Most websites now use what he worked out on that placemat.

dated.title: First .com domain ever registered
dated.detail: symbolics.com. A Lisp Machine company in Cambridge, Mass. The domain still resolves — bought by an investor who keeps it as a museum.

dated.title: Carmack open-sourced the Quake engine
dated.detail: Three years after release, id put the engine's full source online under the GPL. Programmers were soon releasing new versions of it.

undated.title: Karen Spärck Jones introduced IDF in 1972
undated.detail: Inverse Document Frequency. It underlies most modern search engines.

undated.title: grep is named after an ed command
undated.detail: g/re/p: global, regex, print. Ken Thompson already had it as a private tool, and made it public after Doug McIlroy asked for one.

undated.title: Radia Perlman wrote a poem about spanning tree
undated.detail: She published 'Algorhyme' on the protocol she invented. It opens: 'I think that I shall never see / A graph more lovely than a tree.'

undated.title: Alan Kay regretted the term 'objects'
undated.detail: The big idea, he said, was messaging. Of 'objects', a term he'd coined, he wrote in 1998 that 'it gets many people to focus on the lesser idea.'

undated.title: Barbara Liskov built CLU on abstract data types
undated.detail: She's known for the substitution principle. She also led the design of CLU, built on data abstraction: one of the foundations of object-oriented languages like Java and C#.

undated.title: 'Computer' used to be a job title
undated.detail: From the late 1800s, often held by women. They computed ballistic tables, astronomical positions, census results: by hand. The machines took the name from the people they replaced.

undated.title: ENIAC was programmed by six uncredited women
undated.detail: Kathleen Antonelli, Jean Bartik, Frances Spence, Marlyn Meltzer, Ruth Teitelbaum, Frances Holberton. The 1946 press coverage left them out. Recognition came decades later.

undated.title: Women hand-wove Apollo's core rope memory
undated.detail: Each bit was a wire physically threaded through (or around) a tiny magnetic core: the software was the wiring. Errors were very hard to fix once woven.

undated.title: Margaret Hamilton popularized 'software engineering'
undated.detail: She led the Software Engineering Division of MIT's Instrumentation Laboratory for Apollo. The famous 1969 photo shows her with her team's code that sent humans to the Moon.

undated.title: Python is named after Monty Python
undated.detail: Not the snake. Guido was reading Monty Python scripts when he began implementing it. The community kept the in-jokes: 'spam', 'eggs' and 'parrot' all show up in the tutorial.

undated.title: Dijkstra had no use for word processors
undated.detail: He favoured a Montblanc fountain pen and sent photocopies of his numbered EWD notes to colleagues. They photocopied them again, and that's how they spread through computer science.

undated.title: PGP source code was published as a book
undated.detail: Phil Zimmermann challenged US crypto export rules in 1995: he published the full source as a hardback, via MIT Press. Anyone could cut off the covers, scan the pages and build PGP.

undated.title: First webcam was a coffee pot
undated.detail: Cambridge Computer Lab, 1991. Pointed at the Trojan Room coffee pot so researchers wouldn't trek to an empty one. Ran for 10 years. The pot is in a German museum.

undated.title: 1968 Mother of All Demos
undated.detail: Doug Engelbart, in 90 minutes, demoed the mouse, hypertext, video conferencing, real-time collaborative editing, and dynamic file linking.

undated.title: An early secure online purchase: a Sting CD
undated.detail: August 1994. NetMarket. Sting's Ten Summoner's Tales. The transaction used PGP for the credit card.

undated.title: AltaVista's Babelfish
undated.detail: Launched 1997. Free machine translation, named after the Hitchhiker's Guide creature. Grew to 13 languages. It ran until 2012, by then at Yahoo.

undated.title: Your terminal still speaks VT100
undated.detail: Released 1978 by DEC. Its cursor and clear-screen escape sequences are still in use. xterm and its kin are VT100 emulators with extras, like the colour the original never had.

undated.title: Yahoo started as a hand-curated list
undated.detail: Two Stanford grad students, 1994, manually adding new sites to a hierarchy of folders. Originally called 'Jerry and David's Guide to the World Wide Web'. The directory survived until 2014.

undated.title: Plan 9 from Bell Labs
undated.detail: From the group that built Unix. Everything is a file: even network connections, even the window system. Named in homage to the Ed Wood film, and to make marketeers wince.

undated.title: The Story of Mel
undated.detail: 1983 Usenet post by Ed Nather about a programmer who timed his code to a spinning drum memory and wrote a loop with no exit test: it rewrote its own instruction until an overflow turned it into a jump.

undated.title: curl started as a tiny tool called httpget
undated.detail: Daniel Stenberg took it over in 1996 to fetch currency rates. Thirty years later curl runs in cars, fridges, printers, medical devices and espresso machines.

undated.title: BOFH has been running since 1992
undated.detail: Simon Travaglia's Bastard Operator From Hell started on Usenet in 1992 and has appeared in The Register since 2000. The stories moved from a university to an office.

undated.title: RFC 1149: IP over avian carriers
undated.detail: April Fools' RFC from 1990 for carrying IP packets by pigeon. In 2001 the Bergen Linux user group implemented it: nine packets sent over about 3 km, 55% lost, and at least 50 minutes per response.

undated.title: RFC 2324: the coffee pot protocol
undated.detail: April 1998. Hyper Text Coffee Pot Control Protocol. Defines a BREW method and status code 418 'I'm a teapot'. Google uses it as an Easter egg.

undated.title: Knuth pays for errors in hexadecimal dollars
undated.detail: The first to find an error in one of his books earns 0x$1.00: $2.56. He wrote real cheques until fraud stopped him in 2008, and few were cashed. Now it's a deposit at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe.

undated.title: 'lp0 on fire' is a real Linux error
undated.detail: The kernel's parallel printer driver uses it for errors it can't name: not out of paper, not off-line. Michael K. Johnson turned a joking code comment into the message in the 1990s. It's still in drivers/char/lp.c.

undated.title: Bechtolsheim wrote a cheque to a company that didn't exist
undated.detail: August 1998. $100,000 to 'Google Inc.' before incorporation. Page and Brin had to register the company to deposit it. Bechtolsheim had co-founded Sun in 1982.

undated.title: Anders Hejlsberg shaped four eras of programming
undated.detail: Wrote Turbo Pascal, out when he was 22. Then chief architect of Delphi, lead architect of C#, co-creator of TypeScript. Still ships code at Microsoft.

undated.title: Bram Moolenaar made Vim charityware
undated.detail: Bram Moolenaar made Vim charityware: if you like it, help children in Uganda. He died in 2023. His charity, ICCF Holland, closed in 2025, and Kuwasha in Canada carries the work on.

undated.title: Fabrice Bellard's output is implausible
undated.detail: QEMU, FFmpeg and TinyCC. The QuickJS JavaScript engine. A pi record of nearly 2.7 trillion digits in 2009, on a desktop PC costing under $3,000. Co-founded a telecoms company, Amarisoft.

undated.title: James Gosling wrote more than Java
undated.detail: Also: a text editor called Emacs for Unix, satellite data acquisition systems, a multiprocessor Unix and several compilers. At Sun, he was lead engineer of the NeWS window system.

undated.title: Wietse Venema wrote Postfix
undated.detail: He's known for the Postfix mail system. He also wrote TCP Wrapper and, with Dan Farmer, produced the security tools SATAN and The Coroner's Toolkit.

undated.title: Eric Allman started sendmail as a student
undated.detail: Berkeley, late 1970s. His delivermail bridged ARPANET, UUCP and the campus network, then grew into sendmail. By the late 1990s it ran most mail servers. He wrote it unpaid, next to his day job.

undated.title: Niklaus Wirth and Wirth's Law
undated.detail: Designed Pascal, Modula, Oberon, and two workstations: Lilith and Ceres. Wirth's Law, which he credited to Martin Reiser in 1995: 'Software is getting slower more rapidly than hardware becomes faster.'

undated.title: Lynn Conway rewrote how chips are designed
undated.detail: Co-authored the 1980 textbook that made VLSI design teachable. Earlier, IBM fired her for transitioning: she started again as a contract programmer and worked her way up to Xerox PARC.

undated.title: Paul Vixie looked after the internet's DNS software
undated.detail: He started maintaining BIND, the Berkeley Internet Name Domain, in 1988 and became the primary author of BIND 8. He also founded MAPS, an anti-spam nonprofit.

undated.title: Jon Postel was the RFC Editor from 1969 to 1998
undated.detail: He held the job until his death at 55. He's also behind the robustness principle, often called Postel's law: be conservative in what you send, be liberal in what you receive.

undated.title: Theo de Raadt and OpenSSH
undated.detail: Theo de Raadt founded and leads both OpenBSD and OpenSSH, from Calgary. He was also a founding member of NetBSD. In 2004 he won the Free Software Award for OpenBSD and OpenSSH.

undated.title: JPEG 2000's wavelet is named after a Belgian
undated.detail: It uses a wavelet from the Cohen-Daubechies-Feauveau family. The middle name is Ingrid Daubechies, a mathematician from Houthalen. She later became the first woman to lead the International Mathematical Union.

undated.title: The Web had a Belgian champion
undated.detail: Robert Cailliau, a Belgian engineer at CERN, co-wrote the 1990 funding proposal for Tim Berners-Lee's Web, became one of its key proponents and helped build the first browser for the Mac.

undated.title: The datagram came from a French network
undated.detail: Louis Pouzin built CYCLADES in 1973 and made the hosts responsible for reliable delivery, keeping the network itself simple. It's the principle TCP/IP was built on.

undated.title: MINIX ended up inside Intel PCs
undated.detail: Intel put a version of Andrew Tanenbaum's MINIX inside its ME-11 management engine. He didn't know until he read a press report. So he wrote Intel an open letter, starting with thanks.

undated.title: Grace Hopper handed out nanoseconds
undated.detail: When admirals asked why satellite links lag, she gave out 30 cm wires: the distance light travels in a nanosecond. A 300-metre coil was her microsecond. Later, grains of pepper were picoseconds.

undated.title: ELIZA surprised its own creator
undated.detail: Joseph Weizenbaum wrote it in 1966: a pattern-matching script imitating a therapist. His secretary reportedly asked him to leave the room so she could talk to it. He was surprised that people saw feelings in a program.

undated.title: AI was going to be a summer project
undated.detail: The 1955 proposal that coined 'artificial intelligence' asked for a 2-month, 10-man study at Dartmouth. McCarthy, Minsky, Shannon and Rochester expected to make a serious dent in machine intelligence over the summer of 1956.

undated.title: MIT's chess program played a philosopher
undated.detail: Richard Greenblatt wrote a chess program at MIT. Seymour Papert arranged a game between it and Hubert Dreyfus, a philosopher who questioned AI. The program won, and the SIGART newsletter printed the game.

undated.title: The first Black CS PhD pioneered real-time co-editing
undated.detail: Clarence Ellis earned his doctorate in 1969. He went on to pioneer operational transformation: the techniques that let many people edit one document in real time.

undated.title: The .com/.edu/.gov scheme came from one team
undated.detail: Elizabeth Feinler ran the ARPANET's information center until 1989. Her group invented WHOIS and the top-level-domain naming still in use: .com, .edu, .gov, .org.

undated.title: Evelyn Berezin built secretaries a word processor
undated.detail: She was often the first or only woman technologist where she worked. Then she founded Redactron, whose Data Secretary was a standalone computerised word processor. She pitched it in Ms. magazine in 1971.

undated.title: The first US woman with a CS PhD was a nun
undated.detail: Sister Mary Kenneth Keller earned it at Wisconsin in 1965, after a summer computing programme at Dartmouth. She went on to found Clarke's computer science department.

undated.title: She had a personal computer at home in 1965
undated.detail: Mary Allen Wilkes wrote LAP6, the operating system for the LINC, from her parents' living room in Baltimore. She later left computing to become a lawyer.

undated.title: SQLite is tested to aviation standards
undated.detail: Avionics makers showed interest, so its developers built a test harness to support DO-178B, the avionics software standard. Ten months of intense work later, in 2009, it hit 100% MC/DC on the SQLite core.

undated.title: Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen designed the cipher behind AES
undated.detail: AES, the encryption standard the US government announced in November 2001, is a variant of Rijndael, designed by two Belgian cryptographers, Joan Daemen and Vincent Rijmen. Fifteen designs were presented and evaluated over a five-year process.

undated.title: Paul Otlet and the Mundaneum
undated.detail: Paul Otlet and Henri La Fontaine, two Belgian lawyers, set out to gather all the world's knowledge on index cards: more than 12 million index cards and documents by the end. In 1934 Otlet drew plans for a network of "electric telescopes" reading from connected libraries. The Mundaneum is now an archive and museum in Mons.

undated.title: Jaap Haartsen and Bluetooth
undated.detail: Dutch engineer Jaap Haartsen worked on Bluetooth at Ericsson in Lund. The name was meant as a placeholder, after the Danish king Harald Bluetooth, proposed in 1997 by Jim Kardach of Intel. It stuck because the trademark search on the alternative, RadioWire, could not be finished in time.

undated.title: Tommy Flowers built Colossus
undated.detail: Tommy Flowers, a Post Office engineer, built Colossus to break the German Lorenz cipher. He paid part of it himself and was granted £1,000 afterwards, which did not cover it. The Official Secrets Act kept him from claiming the work, and it was not fully acknowledged until the 1970s.

undated.title: LEO, the tea-shop computer
undated.detail: J. Lyons and Co., a British tea-shop company, built its own computer, LEO I. Its first business job, bakery valuations, ran on 5 September 1951. Later, shop orders phoned in each afternoon drove the next night's production and delivery schedules.

undated.title: Christopher Strachey's draughts and love letters
undated.detail: Christopher Strachey wrote a draughts program in 1951, first on the Pilot ACE, and by summer 1952 it played a full game at reasonable speed on the Manchester machine. That summer he also wrote a love-letter generator, described as the first example of computer-generated literature.

undated.title: Kathleen Booth and assembly language
undated.detail: Kathleen Booth is credited with co-writing the first assembly language. At Birkbeck College the Booths' team produced three machines between 1947 and 1953: ARC, SEC and APE(X)C. In 1955 the group demonstrated a machine translating a French sentence into English.

undated.title: Steve Shirley and Freelance Programmers
undated.detail: Stephanie Shirley started Freelance Programmers with £6 of capital, to give women with dependents work they could do from home. It had only three male programmers among its first 300 staff. She signed as "Steve" because letters under her real name went unanswered.

undated.title: Susan Kare drew the first Mac icons
undated.detail: Susan Kare drew the first Macintosh icons on graph paper, mocking up commands at 32 by 32 pixels: scissors for cut, a finger for paste. Andy Hertzfeld had asked her in 1982, in exchange for an Apple II. She had no computer-graphics experience.
